Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add just 6 drops of rennet - this cheese relies primarily on acid coagulation.
Cover and let acidify for 24-36 hours at 68-70°F until curd is firm.
Gently ladle curd into tall pyramid molds (about 5 inches tall with pointed top).
Drain for 48 hours at room temperature, turning twice daily.
Unmold and salt all surfaces moderately.
Dry at room temperature for 24 hours.
Transfer to cave or ripening area at 50-55°F, 85-90% humidity.
Turn every other day. Natural blue-gray molds will develop on rind.
Age minimum 4 weeks, longer for stronger flavor.

notes: The tall pointed pyramid shape is unique to this cheese
Very low rennet and long acidification gives distinctive fine texture
Natural rind develops blue-gray molds - this is characteristic
Interior should be slightly chalky with clean, tangy goat flavor

recipes.title: Traditional Provolone Valpadana (Giant Italian Stretched Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Italian stretched-curd cheesemaking
recipes.description: While provolone originated in southern Italy, Provolone Valpadana from the Po Valley became the DOP standard. Made in enormous sizes (up to 100+ kg), it comes in dolce (mild) and piccante (sharp) versions based on rennet type.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 100°F (38°C).
Add starter culture (thermophilic for faster acidification, or natural whey).
Add rennet: calf rennet for dolce (mild), lamb/kid paste for piccante (sharp).
Let set 20-30 minutes until firm.
Cut curds into small pieces.
Stir and raise temperature to 118°F (48°C) over 30 minutes.
Let curds acidify under whey for 3-5 hours until stretchable.
Cut curd mass into strips.
Heat water to 175-185°F (80-85°C).
Stretch and knead curd until smooth and very elastic.
Form into desired shape: cylinder, pear, cone, or salami.
Tie with cord and hang to set shape while still warm.
Cool in cold water, then brine for 12-24 hours.
Hang to age at 55°F with moderate humidity.
Dolce: age 2-3 months. Piccante: age 6 months to 2+ years.

notes: DOP Provolone Valpadana comes in many shapes: salami, melon, pear, cone, cylinder
Traditional giant wheels can weigh 100+ kg and age for years
Lamb/kid rennet creates the enzymes that develop sharp piccante flavor
Smoked provolone is a popular variation
Dolce version melts beautifully; piccante is better for grating

recipes.title: Traditional Pule (Serbian Donkey Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Pule is made from donkey milk at the Zasavica Special Nature Reserve in Serbia. It's one of the world's rarest and most expensive cheeses because donkeys produce very little milk and it takes 25 liters to make 1 kg of cheese.
recipes.description: Extremely rare Serbian cheese from donkey milk - one of the world's most expensive cheeses due to its scarcity.

ingredients.prep_note: extremely rare - goat milk can substitute

instructions.text: Heat donkey milk very gently to 95°F - donkey milk is delicate.
Add lemon juice gradually, stirring gently.
The milk will slowly curdle into very fine, soft curds.
Let rest for 30 minutes.
Very gently ladle curds into a fine cloth-lined mold.
Let drain for several hours - the curds are very delicate.
Salt lightly and serve fresh.
Pule must be eaten fresh - it does not age well.

notes: Donkey milk has very little casein, making cheese extremely difficult
It takes about 25 liters of donkey milk to make 1 kg of pule
The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and very delicate
One of the world's most expensive cheeses due to rarity
If donkey milk is unavailable, this method works with goat milk for a similar texture

recipes.title: Traditional Pultost (Norwegian Caraway Curd Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Norwegian methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: A spreadable sour milk cheese from Norway, pultost is made from soured buttermilk curds mixed with caraway seeds. The texture is soft and spreadable, the flavor tangy and earthy from the caraway. This simple farm cheese has sustained Norwegian families for generations.

instructions.text: Pour buttermilk into heavy pot. Heat slowly over low heat.
As temperature rises, curds will form. Heat to 160°F (71°C) but do not boil.
When curds clearly separate from thin whey, remove from heat.
Pour through fine cheesecloth-lined colander. Let drain 1-2 hours.
Transfer drained curds to bowl. The texture should be like thick cottage cheese.
Add caraway seeds and salt. Mix well.
For creamier texture, mix in a little cream.
Pack into small crock or jar. Press down to remove air pockets.
Cover and refrigerate. The flavor develops over 1-2 days.
Spread on Norwegian flatbread (flatbrød) or crackers. Keeps refrigerated 2 weeks.

notes: Caraway is traditional in many Scandinavian cheeses
Pultost is a farmhouse cheese - every farm had its own variation
Similar to German quark or American cottage cheese
Can be aged further to develop stronger flavors
Often eaten for breakfast with coffee

recipes.title: Traditional Puzzone di Moena (Stinky Cheese of Moena)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Italian washed-rind cheesemaking
recipes.description: One of Italy's most pungent cheeses, Puzzone di Moena ('big stinker') has been made in the Fiemme and Fassa valleys since the 15th century. The powerful aroma belies a surprisingly delicate, sweet interior.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C) and add starter culture.
Ripen for 30 minutes with occasional stirring.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 35-40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently and raise temperature to 110°F (43°C) over 40 minutes.
Continue stirring until curds shrink and firm up.
Drain whey and pack curds firmly into molds.
Press at increasing weights: 10 lbs for 1 hour, 20 lbs for 3 hours, 30 lbs overnight.
Brine for 12-24 hours depending on size.
Prepare wash: mix B. linens culture with small amount of brine.
Age at 55°F with 95% humidity.
Wash rind with bacteria solution every 2-3 days for first month.
Continue washing weekly for 3-6 months total aging.
Rind develops orange-pink color and strong aroma when ready.

notes: The name literally means 'big stinker' in Italian
Despite the powerful aroma, the paste is sweet and mild
Protected by Slow Food Presidia designation
Traditional makers washed with local well water containing natural bacteria

recipes.title: Traditional Qarish (Egyptian Skimmed Milk Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Egyptian village methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: One of Egypt's most ancient cheeses, qarish is made from skimmed sour milk in the Egyptian countryside. After cream is skimmed for butter, the remaining milk is left to naturally sour, then heated to form curds. The resulting low-fat cheese is tangy and crumbly.

ingredients.prep_note: or whole milk with cream skimmed off

instructions.text: Combine skim milk with buttermilk in a jar or crock. Cover loosely.
Leave at room temperature for 24-48 hours until naturally thickened and soured.
The milk should be thick like yogurt and smell pleasantly tangy.
Pour soured milk into pot. Heat gently over low-medium heat.
Stir occasionally as curds begin to form and separate from whey.
Heat to about 175°F (80°C). Curds should be clearly separated.
Pour through cheesecloth-lined colander. Let drain 30 minutes.
Gather cloth and squeeze gently. Salt the curds to taste.
Press lightly in mold or shape by hand. Refrigerate.
Eat fresh within a week. Traditional accompaniments are bread and honey.

notes: Qarish is the poor farmer's cheese - made from leftover skimmed milk
The low fat content makes it very tangy and crumbly
Can be dried further into a harder aged version
Often eaten at breakfast with bread, honey, and mint
The souring process uses natural milk bacteria - no added acid

recipes.title: Traditional Quark (German Fresh Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional German/Austrian cheesemaking
recipes.description: Germany's most consumed dairy product, Quark is a fresh acid-set cheese somewhere between yogurt and cream cheese. Made throughout Central and Eastern Europe for centuries, it's used in everything from cheesecakes to savory dishes.

ingredients.prep_note: optional, tiny amount for firmer curd

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C).
Stir in cultured buttermilk thoroughly.
If using rennet, add just 1-2 drops diluted in water - this is very little.
Cover and let sit at room temperature (70-75°F) for 12-24 hours.
Milk will thicken and gel like yogurt.
When fully set, cut gently into 1-inch cubes (optional - helps draining).
Line colander with butter muslin or tight cheesecloth.
Gently ladle curd into lined colander.
Let drain 4-8 hours until desired consistency.
For smooth quark, blend briefly or pass through fine sieve.
Refrigerate. Use within 1-2 weeks.

recipes.temperature: 86°F (30°C) to start; room temperature to culture
notes: German 'Magerquark' is fat-free; 'Sahnequark' is creamy - adjust with milk fat content
Essential for German cheesecake (Käsekuchen)
Also called 'tvorog' in Russia, 'tvaroh' in Czech
Consistency ranges from pourable to spreadable depending on draining
Naturally tangy - sweeten for desserts or use savory in dips

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo do Pico (Azorean Island Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Made on Pico Island in the Azores since Portuguese settlement. The volcanic island's unique grass gives distinctive flavor.
recipes.description: Azorean island cheese from Pico with a buttery texture and complex flavor influenced by the volcanic island's unique pastures.

instructions.text: Heat fresh milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently and heat to 100°F over 30 minutes.
Drain curds and pack into round mold.
Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes, flip, 30 lbs for 6 hours.
Soak in brine for 6-8 hours.
Age at 55°F, 85% humidity.
Turn every other day.
Ready in 3-6 weeks when paste is smooth and buttery.

notes: The volcanic soil of Pico Island creates unique pasture
Cows graze on grass growing in lava rock walls
Cheese has slightly salty, oceanic notes from island climate
PDO protected - must be made on Pico Island

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo Rabaçal (Central Portugal Mixed Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Portuguese mixed-milk cheesemaking
recipes.description: From the limestone hills of central Portugal, Rabaçal combines sheep and goat milk in an ancient recipe. The region's chalky soil produces aromatic pastures that give the cheese its distinctive character.

instructions.text: Combine sheep's and goat's milk in traditional ratio (approximately 2:1).
Heat mixed milk to 86-90°F (30-32°C).
Add thistle rennet liquid (steeped in warm water).
Let set 40-50 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curds to hazelnut size.
Stir gently and let rest under whey 10 minutes.
Drain and transfer curds to traditional perforated molds.
Press lightly, flipping several times over 4-6 hours.
Salt surfaces by rubbing over 2-3 days.
Age at 50-55°F with 80% humidity for 30-60 days.
Turn every few days, developing natural rind.

notes: DOP protected since 1996
Takes name from village of Rabaçal in Coimbra district
Small wheels traditionally weigh 300-500 grams
Interior is white, semi-soft, with subtle eyes
Flavor balances sheep's richness with goat's tang

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo São Jorge (Azorean Island Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Portuguese island cheesemaking
recipes.description: Brought to the Azores by Flemish settlers in the 15th century, São Jorge cheese evolved in the volcanic island's unique conditions. Made from raw milk of grass-fed cows on lush pastures, it develops sharp, spicy flavors with age.

instructions.text: Heat raw milk to 90°F (32°C).
Add mesophilic culture, stir well, ripen for 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently, let set 40-50 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch cubes - smaller than many cheeses.
Stir gently for 15 minutes, allowing curds to firm.
Raise temperature gradually to 100°F (38°C) over 30 minutes.
Continue stirring until curds are quite firm and release whey easily.
Drain whey and pack curds firmly into large wheel molds.
Press at increasing weights: 10 lbs for 1 hour, 30 lbs for 4 hours, 50 lbs overnight.
Flip during pressing multiple times.
Brine for 24-36 hours.
Air dry for 2-3 days.
Age at 50-55°F with 85% humidity.
Turn twice weekly, brushing rind. Age minimum 4 months, preferably 7+ months.

notes: DOP protected since 1984
Flemish settlers adapted Gouda techniques to Azorean conditions
Volcanic soil creates unique mineral-rich pastures
Young versions are mild; aged São Jorge is spicy and sharp
Traditional wheels can weigh up to 12 kg

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo Serra da Estrela (Portuguese Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Portugal's most famous cheese, made in the Estrela Mountains using cardoon thistle as coagulant since ancient times.
recipes.description: Portuguese sheep cheese with a creamy to runny interior, made with thistle rennet, featuring complex earthy and slightly bitter flavors.

instructions.text: Soak crushed cardoon thistle flowers in 1/4 cup warm water for 2-3 hours.
Strain to get thistle extract.
Heat sheep milk to 82-86°F (lower than typical).
Add thistle extract slowly while stirring.
Let set for 1-2 hours until soft curd forms.
Cut curds gently into large pieces.
Ladle into flat round molds, press very lightly.
Turn several times over 24-48 hours.
Salt surfaces.
Wrap circumference with cloth band (cincho).
Age at 50-55°F, 90% humidity for 4-8 weeks.
Rind wrinkles as interior becomes soft to runny.

notes: Thistle (cardoon) rennet creates the signature soft/runny interior
The cloth band maintains shape as interior softens
Cut off top and scoop out with spoon when ripe
PDO protected - must use specific sheep breeds and thistle

recipes.title: Traditional Queijo Terrincho (Trás-os-Montes Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Portuguese sheep's milk cheesemaking
recipes.description: From the remote Trás-os-Montes region of northeastern Portugal, this sheep's milk cheese takes its name from the Terrincho sheep breed. Made by shepherds following ancient transhumance routes, it represents Portugal's pastoral heritage.

instructions.text: Prepare thistle rennet: steep dried thistle flowers in warm water for several hours.
Heat sheep's milk to 85-90°F (29-32°C) - traditional method uses no added starter.
Add strained thistle rennet liquid, stir gently.
Let set for 45-60 minutes until firm curd forms.
Cut curds by hand or with traditional tools into walnut-sized pieces.
Let curds rest under whey 10-15 minutes.
Gently stir and raise temperature to 100°F (38°C).
When curds are firm, drain and pack into cloth-lined molds.
Press lightly for 2-4 hours, flipping several times.
Dry salt surfaces over 2-3 days.
Age at 50-55°F with 80-85% humidity.
Turn regularly, rubbing rind. Ready in 2-4 months.

notes: DOP protected - must use Terrincho or Churra breed milk
Thistle rennet gives distinctive slightly bitter, herbal notes
Terrincho sheep are an ancient Portuguese breed adapted to harsh terrain
Paste is ivory-white, slightly crumbly, with small eyes
Traditional in regional dishes from Trás-os-Montes

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Añejo (Mexican Aged Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Añejo means 'aged' - this is the Mexican answer to aged Parmesan-style cheeses.
recipes.description: Mexican aged cheese with a firm, crumbly texture and sharp, salty flavor, perfect for grating.

ingredients.prep_note: or part skim for firmer texture

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch cubes.
Stir gently while heating to 102°F over 30 minutes.
Continue stirring until curds are firm.
Drain curds and salt heavily.
Press at 50 lbs for 24 hours.
Air dry for 1 week.
Coat with paprika or chile powder.
Age at 55°F for 3-6 months minimum.

notes: The paprika or chile coating is traditional
Becomes harder and sharper with age
Essential for enchiladas and other Mexican classics
Often called 'queso cotija añejo' or just 'añejo'

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Asadero (Mexican Grilling Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Asadero means 'roaster' - this cheese is made for melting on the grill or in queso fundido.
recipes.description: Mexican stretched-curd cheese with exceptional melting properties, slightly tangy with a buttery flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently while raising to 100°F.
Drain curds and let acidify at room temperature 6-12 hours.
Test stretch in 170°F water - should stretch smoothly.
Stretch in hot water, adding salt as you work.
Form into flat discs about 1/2 inch thick.
Cool in cold water, then refrigerate.
Use within 2 weeks.

notes: Similar to Oaxaca but shaped in flat discs for grilling
Creates beautiful stringy melted cheese
Essential for queso fundido and Northern Mexican grilling
Sometimes braided like Oaxaca

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Blanco (Central American White Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Central American methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: While cattle came to the Americas with Spanish colonizers, queso blanco quickly became embedded in Central American cuisine. This simple acid-set cheese is essential in pupusas, baleadas, and countless other dishes. The technique likely blended Spanish cheesemaking with indigenous cooking traditions.

instructions.text: Heat milk in a large pot over medium heat to 180°F (82°C), stirring occasionally.
Remove from heat. Add lime juice or vinegar slowly while stirring gently.
Curds will form immediately. Let sit 10 minutes.
Line colander with cheesecloth. Pour in curds and whey.
Let drain 15 minutes. Rinse curds briefly with cool water.
Gather cloth corners and squeeze to remove excess moisture.
Transfer curds to bowl. Add salt and mix well.
Pack into mold or shape into a round. Press lightly for 1-2 hours.
Use immediately for pupusas, enchiladas, or slice for sandwiches.
Store refrigerated up to 2 weeks. Does not melt - perfect for frying.

notes: Queso blanco does not melt - it softens but holds shape when heated
Essential in Salvadoran pupusas, Honduran baleadas, and Mexican dishes
Lime juice gives a slightly different flavor than vinegar
Can be crumbled fresh or sliced for grilling
The technique is essentially the same as paneer but with Latin American seasoning

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Blanco (Latin American White Cheese)
recipes.source_note: The simplest cheese of the Americas, made without culture or rennet. Vinegar or citrus provides the acid.
recipes.description: Simple Latin American white cheese that doesn't melt, perfect for frying, grilling, or crumbling on dishes.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 180-190°F, stirring to prevent scorching.
Remove from heat and slowly stir in vinegar or lime juice.
Curds will form immediately and separate from clear whey.
Let sit 10 minutes.
Strain through cheesecloth-lined colander.
Add salt and mix gently.
Gather cloth and hang to drain for 1 hour.
For firmer cheese, press with weight for additional hour.
Cut into cubes for frying or crumble for topping.
Store refrigerated up to 2 weeks.

notes: Does not melt - holds shape when fried or grilled
Perfect for beginners - no cultures or rennet needed
Similar to paneer but slightly different technique
Excellent source of protein in Latin American cuisines

recipes.title: Traditional Queso de Bola (Filipino Christmas Edam)
recipes.source_note: Dutch Edam became essential Filipino Christmas food through the Manila-Acapulco galleon trade. A fusion tradition.
recipes.description: Ball-shaped waxed cheese in the Dutch Edam tradition, now an essential part of Filipino Christmas celebrations.

instructions.text: Remove 10-20% of cream from milk for characteristic texture.
Heat milk to 86°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently while heating to 95°F over 30 minutes.
Drain 1/3 whey, add warm water to wash curds (removes lactose).
Continue stirring at 95°F for 30 more minutes.
Drain and pack curds into ball-shaped mold.
Press at 30 lbs for 30 minutes, 50 lbs for 12 hours.
Soak in brine for 8 hours.
Air dry 1-2 weeks, then coat in red wax.
Age at 55°F for 2-6 months.

notes: Dutch traders brought Edam to the Philippines in the 1600s
Red wax coating became associated with Christmas festivities
Now an essential part of Filipino Noche Buena (Christmas Eve feast)
Often paired with ham and sweet bread (ensaymada)

recipes.title: Traditional Queso de Cabra al Vino (Spanish Wine-Washed Goat)
recipes.source_note: Murcian tradition of washing goat cheese in local red wine, creating a distinctive purple rind and wine-infused flavor.
recipes.description: Spanish goat cheese washed in red wine, creating a beautiful purple-red rind and subtle fruity, tannic notes in the paste.

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes until firm curd.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently and heat to 100°F over 20 minutes.
Drain curds and press into cylindrical mold at 25 lbs for 6 hours.
Flip and press at 40 lbs for 12 hours.
Soak in saturated brine for 12 hours.
Age at 55°F, 85% humidity.
After 1 week, begin washing rind with red wine every 2-3 days.
Continue wine washing for 2-3 months until rind is deep purple.

notes: Local Monastrell or Jumilla wines are traditional for washing
The wine tannins preserve the rind and add flavor
Purple color deepens with longer aging and more wine washes
Interior remains white to pale yellow, with subtle wine notes

recipes.title: Traditional Queso de Murcia al Vino (Spanish Wine-Washed Goat Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Murcian methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: A distinctive cheese from Spain's Murcia region, made from Murciano-Granadina goat milk and washed with local red wine during aging. The wine creates a deep burgundy rind and imparts subtle fruity notes. Sometimes called 'Drunken Goat' cheese in export markets.

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 86°F (30°C). Add calcium chloride, then culture. Ripen 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and stir gently. Let set 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes, then stir gently for 20 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 95°F (35°C) over 20 minutes while stirring.
Drain whey. Pack curds into cylindrical molds. Press with 15 lbs for 6 hours, flipping every 2 hours.
Remove from mold. Brine in salt solution for 4-6 hours.
Air dry for 2-3 days until surface is dry to touch.
Begin wine washing: pour wine into shallow dish and turn cheese in it, coating all surfaces.
Age at 55°F (13°C) and 85% humidity. Wash with wine every 3-4 days for first month, then weekly.
Age 2-3 months total. The rind will be deep purple-red, the paste ivory and smooth.

notes: The wine washing creates a distinctive color and subtle flavor
Queso de Murcia (without wine) also has PDO protection
Murciano-Granadina goats produce especially rich milk
The finished cheese has mild, slightly sweet goat flavor with wine notes
Often marketed as 'Drunken Goat' or 'Borracho' cheese

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Fresco (Mexican Fresh Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Brought by Spanish colonizers, adapted with local techniques. Essential to Mexican cuisine from tacos to enchiladas.
recipes.description: Mexican fresh cheese that crumbles easily, with a mild milky flavor and slight tang, used throughout Mexican cooking.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 180-185°F, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching.
Remove from heat.
Add vinegar slowly while stirring gently.
Curds will form and separate from whey within minutes.
Let rest 10 minutes for curds to consolidate.
Line colander with cheesecloth, ladle in curds.
Sprinkle salt over curds, mix gently.
Tie cheesecloth and hang to drain for 1-2 hours.
For firmer cheese, press in mold with light weight for 1 hour.
Refrigerate and use within 1-2 weeks.

notes: Does not melt when heated - perfect for sprinkling on hot dishes
Lime juice gives more authentic flavor than vinegar
Can be made from any milk including goat
Essential topping for elote, tacos, tostadas, and enchiladas

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Majorero (Canary Islands Goat Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Made by the Majos (indigenous Guanches) before Spanish conquest. Uses milk from the Majorera goat unique to the island.
recipes.description: Canary Islands goat cheese from Fuerteventura with a distinctive palm leaf pattern, ranging from mild when young to sharp when aged.

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 86°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into small pieces.
Stir gently while heating to 100°F over 20 minutes.
Drain curds and pack into molds with palm leaf (pleita) pattern.
Press at 30 lbs for 6 hours, 50 lbs for 12 hours.
Soak in brine for 24 hours.
Age at 55°F, 85% humidity.
Rub rind with olive oil mixed with pimentón (or gofio).
Age 2 months (tierno), 4 months (semi-curado), or 6+ months (curado).

notes: The Majorera goat is native only to Fuerteventura
Pre-Hispanic Majos people made this cheese before Spanish arrival
Rind can be rubbed with paprika (red), gofio (yellow), or oil (natural)
PDO protected since 1996

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Oaxaca (Mexican String Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Oaxacan methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: Mexico's beloved string cheese from Oaxaca, made using pasta filata (stretched curd) technique that arrived with Spanish colonizers. The cheese is stretched into long ribbons and wound into balls. It melts beautifully, making it essential for quesadillas and tlayudas.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Add calcium chloride and stir. Add culture and ripen 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet. Stir gently for 30 seconds. Let set 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curd into 1/2-inch cubes. Let rest 5 minutes.
Slowly raise temperature to 100°F (38°C) while stirring gently. Hold 30 minutes.
Drain whey. Place curds in warm whey at 100°F to acidify 2-4 hours until stretching test passes.
Test: place small piece in 170°F water. If it stretches smooth without breaking, curds are ready.
Heat water to 170°F (77°C). Cut curd into strips and submerge.
Work the curd, stretching and folding until smooth and shiny. Stretch into long ribbons.
Wind the ribbons into balls while still warm and pliable. Drop into ice water to set shape.
Salt by rubbing or brief brine. Store refrigerated up to 2 weeks.

notes: Queso Oaxaca is Mexico's most popular melting cheese
The technique came from Spain/Italy but was adapted to local tastes
Properly made Oaxaca cheese pulls into long strings when melted
Essential for quesadillas, tlayudas, and stuffed peppers
Called quesillo in Oaxaca; elsewhere in Mexico it's queso Oaxaca

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Palmero (Canary Islands Smoked)
recipes.source_note: Made by the Guanche people before Spanish conquest. Smoked over almond shells and prickly pear wood.
recipes.description: Canary Islands goat cheese from La Palma, traditionally smoked over almond shells and prickly pear, with a distinctive smoky flavor.

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 88°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 1 hour.
Cut curds into small pieces.
Stir and heat gently to 95°F over 20 minutes.
Drain curds and pack into cylindrical mold.
Press at 25 lbs for 4 hours, flip, 40 lbs for 12 hours.
Soak in brine for 24 hours.
Air dry for 1-2 weeks until firm surface.
Cold smoke with almond shells for 2-3 weeks, a few hours each day.
Age at 55°F for 3-6 months total.

notes: Pre-Hispanic Guanche people made cheese before Spanish arrival
Traditional smoking uses almond shells and prickly pear wood
PDO protected - must be from La Palma goats
Exterior darkens from smoking; interior remains white to ivory

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Panela (Mexican Basket Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Named for the basket molds (canastas) used to shape it. A fresh, mild cheese popular throughout Mexico.
recipes.description: Mexican fresh cheese with a smooth texture and basket-weave imprint, absorbs flavors well and softens when heated.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture, stir, and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add diluted rennet and stir gently for 30 seconds.
Let set for 45 minutes until clean break.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently for 15 minutes at 90°F.
Drain curds and add salt.
Pack into basket-weave molds (or colander for similar effect).
Let drain at room temperature for 4-6 hours.
Refrigerate and use within 2 weeks.

notes: The basket weave imprint is characteristic of authentic panela
Softens when heated but doesn't fully melt
Great for absorbing marinades and salsas
Often served as an appetizer with herbs and chilies

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Tetilla (Galician Breast Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Spanish regional cheesemaking
recipes.description: Named for its distinctive breast-like shape (tetilla means 'small breast'), this mild Galician cheese has ancient Celtic origins. Creamy and slightly tangy, it's one of Spain's most popular table cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86-90°F (30-32°C).
Add mesophilic culture, ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 45-60 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch pieces.
Stir gently without raising temperature.
Drain and pack curds into breast-shaped molds.
Press lightly to maintain soft texture.
Turn frequently during first 24 hours.
Brine for 12-24 hours or dry salt.
Age at 50-55°F with 85% humidity.
Ready in 2-4 weeks when interior is creamy.

notes: DOP protected since 1992
The conical shape was traditionally formed by hanging in cloth
Celtic origins - Galicia has strong Celtic heritage
Mild, creamy, slightly tangy flavor
Pairs well with Galician Albariño wine

recipes.title: Traditional Queso Zamorano (Spanish Hard Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Zamoran methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: From the province of Zamora in Castile and León comes this hard sheep's milk cheese with origins predating Roman times. Made exclusively from Churra and Castellana sheep milk, it's pressed in traditional esparto grass molds that leave a distinctive zigzag pattern on the rind.

instructions.text: Heat sheep milk to 86°F (30°C). Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized.
Add thermophilic culture and ripen for 45 minutes.
Add rennet (lamb rennet paste is traditional) and let set for 30-45 minutes.
Cut curds into very small pieces - rice-sized for hard cheese.
Slowly raise temperature to 104°F (40°C) over 30 minutes, stirring continuously.
Hold at 104°F for another 30-45 minutes, stirring, until curds are very firm.
Drain whey. Pack curds tightly into zigzag-patterned molds (or use cheese mold with mat).
Press with heavy weight (40-50 lbs) for 24 hours, flipping every 6 hours.
Brine for 24-48 hours in saturated salt solution.
Age at 50-55°F (10-13°C) and 85% humidity for minimum 6 months, up to 2 years. Rub with olive oil.

notes: Protected by Denominación de Origen (DO) since 1992
Traditional molds are woven from esparto grass creating zigzag pattern
Minimum aging is 6 months; artisanal versions age 2+ years
Flavor is intense, complex, slightly piquant with lanolin notes
Often compared to Manchego but with distinctive character from Churra sheep

recipes.title: Traditional Raclette (Swiss Melting Cheese)
recipes.source_note: The word 'raclette' comes from 'racler' meaning to scrape. Alpine herders melted this cheese by the fire for centuries.
recipes.description: Swiss alpine cheese made for melting and scraping onto potatoes and pickles, with a smooth creamy texture and nutty flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add thermophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 35 minutes until firm.
Cut curds to corn kernel size.
Stir gently while heating to 104°F over 30 minutes.
Continue stirring at 104°F for 30 more minutes.
Drain curds and transfer to large round mold.
Press at 25 lbs for 30 minutes, flip, 40 lbs for 12 hours.
Soak in saturated brine for 48 hours.
Age at 55°F, 95% humidity.
Wash rind with brine every few days during aging.
Age 3-6 months until paste is supple and aromatic.

notes: Traditional raclette is made on alpine pastures during summer
The washed rind creates the characteristic aroma
When heated, it melts smoothly without becoming stringy
Served by melting against a fire and scraping onto plates

recipes.title: Traditional Ragusano (Sicilian Rectangular Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Sicilian stretched-curd cheesemaking
recipes.description: A unique rectangular stretched-curd cheese from Ragusa province in Sicily, Ragusano has been made since at least the 1500s. Its distinctive rectangular shape comes from being pressed between boards - unusual for pasta filata cheese.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C).
Add acidic whey starter.
Add lamb rennet paste dissolved in water, let set 30-40 minutes.
Break curd using traditional 'rotula' tool into small pieces.
Let curds acidify under whey for 18-24 hours until pH reaches 5.0-5.2.
Cut acidified curd mass into strips.
Heat water to 175°F (80°C).
Stretch curd strips in hot water until very elastic.
Form into large rectangular mass.
Place between two wooden boards (traditional 'mastredda' molds).
Press and turn regularly for 24-48 hours to form rectangular shape.
Brine for 24-48 hours depending on size.
Age hanging by rope in ventilated rooms.
Rub rind with olive oil periodically during 4-12 month aging.

notes: DOP protected - one of Sicily's oldest and most prestigious cheeses
Modicana is an ancient Sicilian cattle breed that nearly went extinct
Traditional blocks weigh 10-16 kg (22-35 lbs)
Young cheese is mild; aged versions develop complex, slightly piquant flavor
Grated over Sicilian pasta dishes like pasta alla Norma

recipes.title: Traditional Reblochon (Savoyard Farmer's Secret Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Savoyard methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: Born of peasant tax evasion in the 13th century, Reblochon was made from the 'second milking' - after the tax collector had measured the herd's output, farmers would milk again. This rich, creamy, second-milk cheese became the heart of tartiflette. The name comes from 'reblocher' (to pinch again).

instructions.text: Combine milk and cream. Heat to 95°F (35°C). Add calcium chloride and culture. Ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet. Let set 30-40 minutes until soft clean break.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes (larger curds for creamy texture). Let rest 10 minutes.
Very gently stir for 10 minutes at 95°F. Keep curds large and moist.
Drain whey. Ladle curds into small round molds (about 3-4 inches). Do not press.
Flip every 30 minutes for 3 hours. Let drain overnight at room temperature.
Salt surfaces lightly. Begin aging at 55°F (13°C) and 95% humidity.
Wash gently with brine every 2-3 days. A yellowish-pink rind will develop.
Age 3-4 weeks. Interior becomes creamy and slightly runny near rind.
Essential ingredient in tartiflette - baked with potatoes, bacon, and onions.

notes: Invented by farmers hiding milk production from tax collectors
Second milking was richer because less volume, more fat
Has PDO protection - must be made in specific Savoie areas
Fermier Reblochon (farm-made) is distinguished by green casein mark
Tartiflette was invented in 1980s to promote Reblochon sales

recipes.title: Traditional Reblochon (Savoyard Washed-Rind)
recipes.source_note: Name comes from 'reblocher' (to milk again). Farmers hid the richest milk from tax collectors, then made cheese.
recipes.description: French washed-rind cheese from the Alps with a creamy interior and earthy, nutty flavor. Essential for tartiflette.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and B. linens. Ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently for 15 minutes at 90°F - do not heat further.
Ladle curds into flat round molds (5-inch diameter).
Turn frequently for 6-8 hours as cheese drains.
Salt all surfaces.
Age at 55°F, 95% humidity.
Wash with light brine every 2-3 days.
Age 4-6 weeks until rind is orange-pink and paste is creamy.

notes: The 'rebloche' or second milking is richer in fat
Farmers would under-report milk to avoid taxes, then make cheese with the hidden portion
Essential ingredient for tartiflette (Savoyard potato dish)
AOC protected since 1958

recipes.title: Traditional Reblochon (Tartiflette Alpine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional French alpine cheesemaking
recipes.description: Born from medieval tax evasion, Reblochon comes from 're-blocher' meaning 'to milk again.' Farmers would incompletely milk cows during tax assessments, then fully milk them afterwards for this rich, creamy cheese.

ingredients.prep_note: high fat content, ideally second milking

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C). Traditionally made from second, richer milking.
Add mesophilic culture and P. candidum. Ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently, let set 30-40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently for 10 minutes - do NOT heat curds further.
Drain most whey, leaving curds quite wet.
Ladle wet curds into small molds (traditional size is 3.5 inches diameter).
Press very lightly - just enough to consolidate. Heavy pressing ruins texture.
Flip after 1 hour, then again after 2 hours.
Press casein label into top surface (traditional identification mark).
Salt surfaces lightly or brief brine for 30 minutes.
Age at 55°F with 95% humidity.
Wash with light brine every 2-3 days for first week, then once weekly.
Ready when rind is pinkish-orange and interior is soft and creamy, about 4-6 weeks.

notes: AOC protected since 1958, must be made from raw milk in Haute-Savoie
Green casein label = fermier (farmstead); red label = fruitier (cooperative)
Essential ingredient in tartiflette, the Savoyard potato dish
Should be soft and yielding when pressed - not runny but not firm
Best eaten at room temperature when interior is almost flowing

recipes.title: Traditional Red Leicester (Annatto-Colored Cheddar)
recipes.source_note: Traditional English territorial cheesemaking
recipes.description: A Leicester variation of the cheddar family, Red Leicester gets its distinctive orange-red color from annatto. Developed in the 17th century partly to differentiate it from other cheeses in the market, it has a mellow, nutty flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C).
Add annatto - use more than for Gloucester to achieve deep red-orange color.
Add mesophilic culture, ripen 45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir and raise temperature to 100°F (38°C) over 40 minutes.
Continue stirring until curds are quite firm.
Drain whey, pile curds, let acidify 15-20 minutes.
Mill curds, salt thoroughly.
Pack into molds, press heavily overnight.
Bandage with cloth or wax.
Age at 55°F with 85% humidity for 3-9 months.

notes: The vivid color originally helped identify Leicester cheese at market
Annatto is a natural plant-based coloring from achiote seeds
Texture is slightly more open and moist than cheddar
Matures faster than cheddar - nice at 3-6 months
Melts beautifully - excellent for Welsh rarebit

recipes.title: Traditional Requesón (Mexican Whey Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Mexican version of ricotta, made from the whey of other cheeses. Waste not, want not.
recipes.description: Mexican fresh whey cheese, creamy and mild, used in sweet and savory dishes throughout Mexico.

instructions.text: Start with fresh, warm whey immediately after making cheese.
Add milk if using for richer requesón.
Heat slowly to 185-195°F, stirring occasionally.
When foam and fine curds appear, add vinegar slowly.
Curds will rise to surface.
Remove from heat and let rest 10 minutes.
Skim curds into cheesecloth-lined strainer.
Add salt and mix gently.
Drain for 1 hour.
Use fresh within 1 week.

notes: Never waste whey - it makes delicious requesón
Traditional in Mexican breakfast tacos and pastries
Sweeter and milder than Italian ricotta
Can be used in enchiladas, quesadillas, or desserts

recipes.title: Traditional Robiola (Piedmont Fresh Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Name may come from Latin 'rubeum' (red) for the reddish rind, or from town of Robbio.
recipes.description: Piedmontese fresh to soft-ripened cheese made from various milks, with a creamy texture and mild, tangy flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk(s) to 90°F.
Add cultures and ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 1 hour.
Cut curds into 1-inch pieces.
Let rest 10 minutes.
Gently ladle into small round or square molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24-48 hours.
Salt lightly.
FOR FRESH: Eat within 1 week.
FOR AGED: Age at 55°F, 90% humidity for 2-4 weeks until rind forms.

notes: Many varieties exist: Robiola di Roccaverano (goat, DOP), Robiola Bosina (cow/sheep)
Can be eaten fresh or aged with bloomy rind
Traditional to wrap aged versions in leaves
One of Piedmont's most beloved cheeses

recipes.title: Traditional Robiola Piemontese (Piedmont Soft-Ripened Cheese)
recipes.attribution: Ancient Piedmontese tradition, possibly Celtic origin
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Piedmontese methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: A family of soft, surface-ripened cheeses from Piedmont with roots possibly dating to Celtic times. The name may come from Latin 'rubrum' (red) for the reddish rind, or from the town of Robbio. Made from cow, sheep, or goat milk (or mixes), robiola is creamy to runny when ripe.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 72°F (22°C) - room temperature. Add cultures and Penicillium candidum. Stir well.
Add just 2 drops of rennet (this is a lactic-set cheese, mostly acid-coagulated).
Cover and let set for 18-24 hours at room temperature. Curd will be very soft and yogurt-like.
Gently ladle curd into small molds (no cheesecloth needed). Do not break up the curd.
Let drain at room temperature for 24 hours, flipping once or twice.
The cheese will shrink significantly as whey drains.
Remove from mold, salt lightly on all surfaces.
Place on draining mat in ripening container. Maintain 55°F (13°C) and 90% humidity.
White mold will develop over 5-7 days. Flip daily.
Ripen for 1-2 weeks until surface is fully covered and interior begins to soften. Eat at peak ripeness.

notes: Robiola is a slow, lactic-set cheese - the long set develops acidity naturally
Multiple milk types create different flavor profiles
Robiola di Roccaverano (goat only) has DOP protection
Properly ripened robiola is creamy to oozy under a thin white rind
Small format cheese - traditionally individual-serving sized

recipes.title: Traditional Roncal (Navarra Aged Sheep Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Spanish Pyrenean cheesemaking
recipes.description: Spain's first DOP cheese (1981), Roncal comes from the Roncal Valley in the Navarrese Pyrenees. Documented since at least the 13th century, it's made only from December to July when sheep graze the valley's lush pastures.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 86-90°F (30-32°C).
Add starter culture, ripen 30 minutes.
Add lamb rennet, let set 30-40 minutes.
Cut curds very small, to rice grain size.
Stir and raise temperature to 100-104°F (38-40°C).
Continue stirring until curds are very dry and firm.
Drain whey completely.
Pack curds very firmly into cylindrical molds.
Press heavily for 24 hours, flipping multiple times.
Rub rind with dry salt over several days (traditional method).
Age at 50-55°F with 80-85% humidity.
Turn and brush regularly. Minimum 4 months, preferably 7-12 months.

notes: Spain's first DOP cheese, protected since 1981
Made only in seven villages of the Roncal Valley
Production restricted to December-July milking season
Hard, dense texture with granular paste
Intense, piquant flavor - sharper than Manchego

recipes.title: Traditional Roquefort (King of Blue Cheeses)
recipes.source_note: Traditional French blue cheesemaking
recipes.description: Perhaps the world's most famous blue cheese, Roquefort has been made in the caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon for over 2,000 years. Legend says a shepherd left his lunch in a cave and returned to find the first Roquefort.

instructions.text: Heat sheep's milk to 86°F (30°C).
Add mesophilic culture and P. roqueforti. Ripen 60-90 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 60-90 minutes for soft curd.
Cut curds into large 1-inch cubes - handle very gently.
Let curds rest, then ladle into molds without pressing.
Drain naturally 3-5 days, flipping regularly.
Salt surfaces generously over several days.
Pierce cheese with needles to create air channels for blue mold.
Age in natural caves or cave-like conditions (45°F, 95% humidity).
Blue veins develop over 3-4 weeks after piercing.
Wrap in foil to slow mold growth once desired blueing achieved.
Minimum 3 months aging; up to 9 months for stronger flavor.

notes: AOC protected since 1925 - France's first protected cheese
Must be aged in natural Combalou caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon
The caves have natural 'fleurines' (fissures) that regulate temperature and humidity
Lacaune sheep breed is required - milk is very rich
Sharp, tangy, salty with creamy texture and blue-green veins

recipes.title: Traditional Roquefort (French King of Blues)
recipes.source_note: Legend says a shepherd left bread and sheep cheese in a cave while pursuing a maiden. Mentioned by Pliny the Elder in 79 AD.
recipes.description: French sheep milk blue cheese aged in the natural caves of Roquefort, with creamy texture and sharp, tangy blue flavor.

instructions.text: Heat sheep milk to 86°F.
Add mesophilic culture and P. roqueforti. Ripen 1 hour.
Add lamb rennet and let set for 2 hours.
Cut curds into large 1-inch cubes.
Let curds rest 15 minutes, then gently ladle into cylindrical molds.
Do not press - allow to drain naturally for 3-5 days, turning regularly.
Dry salt all surfaces.
Age at 45-50°F in very humid conditions (95%+).
Pierce with needles after 3-4 weeks for air to reach mold.
Age in cave conditions for 3-6 months.
Wrap in foil to stop further bluing when desired level reached.

notes: First cheese granted AOC protection in France (1925)
Must be aged in natural caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon
The P. roqueforti spores come from bread left in the caves
Sheep milk only - any cow milk disqualifies it as Roquefort

recipes.title: Traditional Rubing (Chinese Goat Cheese Cubes)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Sani Yi minority methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: Another of China's rare indigenous cheeses, rubing comes from the Sani subgroup of the Yi minority in Yunnan's Stone Forest region. Made from goat milk, it's formed into small cubes and pan-fried until golden. The mild, squeaky texture is similar to halloumi.

ingredients.prep_note: cow milk works but goat is traditional

instructions.text: Heat goat milk to 185°F (85°C), stirring occasionally.
Remove from heat. Add acid whey or vinegar while stirring gently. Curds will form immediately.
Let sit 10 minutes for curds to consolidate.
Pour through cheesecloth-lined colander. Let drain 10 minutes.
Gather cloth and squeeze to remove more whey. Mix in salt.
Press cheese in small square mold or shape by hand into a block.
Press with moderate weight for 2 hours or until quite firm.
Cut block into 1-inch cubes. These can be stored refrigerated for a few days.
To serve: pan-fry cubes in a little oil over medium heat until golden on all sides.
Serve hot with dipping sauce or as part of Yunnan-style hot pot.

notes: Rubing is specifically a Sani Yi minority cheese from Shilin (Stone Forest) area
The texture is squeaky like halloumi or fresh cheese curds
Must be eaten fried - not typically eaten raw
Often served with a spicy dipping sauce in Yunnan restaurants
The Sani have made this cheese for generations alongside their goat herding

recipes.title: Traditional Rubing (Yunnan Goat Cheese Cubes)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Chinese minority cheesemaking
recipes.description: Made by the Sani people (Yi ethnic group) in Yunnan's Stone Forest region, Rubing is fresh goat cheese pressed into dense cubes. Often grilled until golden brown, it's one of China's most distinctive traditional cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat goat's milk to 175°F (80°C), stirring occasionally.
Slowly pour in acid while stirring gently.
Continue stirring as curds form and separate from whey.
Remove from heat when curds are well formed.
Strain through cloth, letting whey drain.
While still warm, knead curds to make smooth.
Press into square or rectangular molds.
Press with weights for 1-2 hours until very firm.
Unmold and cut into small cubes (about 1-inch).
Eat fresh, or grill/pan-fry until golden brown.

notes: Rubing means 'milk cake' in Chinese
The Sani have made this cheese for generations
Traditionally grilled over charcoal and eaten with salt and chili
Dense, chewy texture that holds up well to grilling
Best eaten very fresh - does not store long

recipes.title: Traditional Rushan (Chinese Bai Minority Fan-Shaped Cheese)
recipes.attribution: Bai ethnic minority, Yunnan Province, China
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Bai minority methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: One of China's rare traditional cheeses, rushan (meaning 'milk fan') is made by the Bai minority in Yunnan Province. The stretchy curd is wrapped around bamboo sticks and dried into fan-like shapes. When fried and dusted with sugar, it becomes a beloved Yunnan street snack.

ingredients.prep_note: or 1/4 cup white vinegar mixed with water

instructions.text: Heat milk to 150°F (65°C) in a large wok or wide pan. The shallow shape is traditional.
Slowly add acidic whey or diluted vinegar while stirring. Curds will form and stretch.
Keep stirring over heat as the curds become stretchy like mozzarella. This takes 15-20 minutes.
When curd forms a stretchy mass, use chopsticks to lift and stretch it repeatedly.
Take a portion of the stretched curd and wrap it around a bamboo stick in overlapping layers.
Spread and flatten the wrapped curd into a thin, fan-like shape on the stick.
Repeat with remaining curd. Place sticks in sun or well-ventilated area to dry for 2-3 days.
Dried rushan becomes stiff and can be stored for months.
To serve: heat oil and fry dried rushan until puffed and golden. Dust with sugar while hot.
Can also be grilled over charcoal, which is the street food method in Dali, Yunnan.

notes: Rushan is one of very few indigenous Chinese cheese traditions
The Bai people of Dali have made this for generations using water buffalo milk
Fresh rushan (before drying) is also eaten, similar to mozzarella
Street vendors in Dali grill rushan over charcoal and add various toppings
The cheese-making tradition likely came via ancient trade routes

recipes.title: Traditional Rushan (Chinese Bai Fan Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Chinese minority cheesemaking
recipes.description: A unique Chinese cheese from the Bai people of Yunnan province, Rushan ('milk fan') is stretched cheese dried in thin fan-shaped sheets. It represents rare cheesemaking tradition in a country not known for dairy.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 140°F (60°C).
Slowly add acid (traditionally papaya juice) while stirring.
Continue heating and stirring as curds form.
When curds fully separate, drain off whey.
Knead curds while still warm until smooth and elastic.
Using two sticks, stretch curd into thin sheet like pulling taffy.
Wrap stretched sheet around one stick, continue pulling.
Fan out into thin, semi-circular 'fan' shape.
Drape over bamboo rack to dry.
Dry until firm but still pliable (few hours to overnight).
Can be eaten fresh, grilled, or deep-fried.

notes: Rushan means 'milk fan' describing the shape
One of China's only indigenous stretched-curd cheeses
Papaya enzyme (papain) was traditional coagulant
Popular street food in Dali - often wrapped around sweet fillings
Can be grilled until golden and slightly crispy

recipes.title: Traditional Saint-Nectaire (Volcanic Mountain Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Named after the town of Saint-Nectaire. Louis XIV's court favorite. Made on volcanic Auvergne pastures.
recipes.description: Washed-rind Auvergnat cheese with a grey-brown natural rind, supple texture, and earthy mushroom flavors.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently at 90°F for 15 minutes.
Drain curds and pack into flat round molds.
Press at 25 lbs for 12 hours.
Salt surfaces.
Age on rye straw at 50°F, 95% humidity.
Turn every 2-3 days. Natural molds develop grey-brown rind.
Age 4-8 weeks until interior is supple.

notes: Became famous when served at court of Louis XIV
Traditional aging on rye straw contributes to rind character
Volcanic pastures of Mont Dore create distinctive terroir
AOC distinguishes Fermier (farm) from Laitier (dairy)

recipes.title: Traditional Sainte-Maure de Touraine (French Log Cheese)
recipes.source_note: One of the oldest French goat cheeses, traditionally made since the Arab invasions brought goats to France. The straw through the center is its trademark.
recipes.description: Log-shaped French goat cheese with a distinctive straw running through its center, ash-coated exterior, and creamy tangy interior.

instructions.text: Warm goat milk to 68-70°F.
Add all cultures and stir gently to distribute.
Add calcium chloride if using pasteurized milk.
Add small amount of diluted rennet.
Cover and let acidify for 18-24 hours until curd is firm.
Place sterilized rye straw lengthwise in log-shaped molds.
Carefully ladle curd into molds around the straw.
Drain for 24-48 hours, turning carefully to avoid disturbing straw.
Unmold gently - straw should remain centered in the log.
Salt all surfaces, then coat with vegetable ash.
Age at 52-55°F, 85-90% humidity, turning every other day.
Ready in 3-4 weeks when rind is established and paste is creamy.

notes: The straw serves dual purpose: structural support during aging and proof of authenticity
Traditional straw is rye, burned with the producer's ID for AOC cheeses
Arabs brought goats to the Loire Valley in the 8th century after the Battle of Poitiers
Interior texture changes from chalky to creamy as it ripens from outside in

recipes.title: Traditional Salers (Auvergne Raw Milk Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Made only during summer grazing season (May-October) from Salers cattle. The strictest AOC rules of any French cheese.
recipes.description: Raw milk Auvergnat cheese made on-farm during summer grazing, with robust earthy flavor and firm texture.

ingredients.prep_note: must be milked in presence of calf

instructions.text: Milk Salers cow with calf present (required by AOC).
Transfer warm milk immediately to gerle (traditional wooden vat).
Add whey starter from previous batch.
Add rennet and let set for 1 hour.
Break curds and heat to 100°F while stirring.
Drain whey and press curds in cloth.
Let rest 12-24 hours (tomme stage).
Break up tomme, add salt, let rest again.
Pack into large molds (35-50 kg traditional).
Press heavily for 48 hours.
Age at 50°F, 95% humidity for minimum 3 months.
Brush rind regularly. Age up to 18 months for full flavor.

notes: Strictest AOC in France - must be farm-made during summer grazing
Salers cattle only let down milk with calf present
Traditional gerle (wooden vat) adds wild cultures
Tomme Fraîche de Salers is the fresh curd used in aligot

recipes.title: Traditional Salers (Transhumance Mountain Cheese)
recipes.attribution: French tradition from Auvergne, ancient transhumance
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Auvergnat methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: A close relative of Cantal but made only during summer when cattle graze high mountain pastures (transhumance). Salers must be made from raw milk of Salers cattle and only between April and November. The wild flowers and herbs of the volcanic pastures flavor the milk.

ingredients.prep_note: ideally from Salers cows on pasture

instructions.text: Use fresh raw milk, still warm from milking if possible. Add culture if desired and ripen 20 minutes.
Add diluted rennet. Let set 45-60 minutes until firm break.
Cut curds into small pieces. Stir gently while raising temperature to 98°F (37°C).
Continue stirring at 98°F for 30 minutes until curds are firm.
Drain whey. Pack curds into mold and press with 30 lbs for 8 hours.
Remove and mill the pressed tome into pieces. Salt and let rest 2 hours.
Repack and press with 50 lbs for 24-48 hours.
Traditional Salers is pressed in a 'gerle' - a wooden barrel. Use lined mold at home.
Remove, rub with salt, and air dry 3-5 days.
Age at 50°F (10°C) and 90% humidity for minimum 3 months, traditionally 12-18 months.

notes: Salers can only be made April-November during mountain grazing
Must use raw milk from Salers cattle - a hardy breed from Auvergne
The gerle (wooden barrel) develops unique microflora over generations
Salers Tradition uses ONLY milk from Salers cows; regular Salers allows other breeds
Has PDO protection with strict requirements

recipes.title: Traditional Sbrinz (Swiss Ancient Hard Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Possibly Switzerland's oldest cheese, traded over the Gotthard Pass. May predate Parmesan.
recipes.description: Swiss extra-hard cheese traditionally shaved rather than grated, with intense aromatic flavor after 18+ months aging.

instructions.text: Heat fresh alpine milk to 90°F.
Add thermophilic culture and ripen 20 minutes.
Add calf rennet and let set for 30-35 minutes.
Cut curds very fine, to rice-grain size.
Cook while stirring continuously, raising to 135°F over 45 minutes.
Hold at 135°F, stirring, for 30 more minutes.
Let curds settle briefly, then transfer to mold.
Press at 50 lbs for 1 hour, 80 lbs for 12-24 hours.
Soak in brine for 3-4 weeks.
Age first 6 months at 60°F, 85% humidity.
Then age 12-30 more months at 55°F, 75% humidity.
Ready minimum 18 months, traditionally 2-3 years.

notes: May predate Parmesan as one of the oldest alpine hard cheeses
Traditionally shaved thin with a special knife (hobelkäse)
The highest cooking temperature of any Swiss cheese
Once important trade good over the Gotthard and Splügen passes

recipes.title: Traditional Sbrinz (Swiss Ancient Hard Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Swiss hard cheesemaking
recipes.description: One of Europe's oldest cheeses, Sbrinz may date to Roman times when it was traded across the Alps. This extremely hard Swiss cheese is traditionally shaved into thin curls called 'Möckli' and can age for several years.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C).
Add thermophilic culture, ripen 15-20 minutes.
Add rennet, let set 25-30 minutes.
Cut curds extremely fine - smaller than rice grains.
Stir continuously while raising temperature to 133°F (56°C) - very high.
Continue stirring for 45-60 minutes until curds are very dry.
Press curds under whey briefly.
Transfer to molds, press very heavily for 24 hours.
Brine for 3-4 weeks.
Age standing on edge (not flat) at 60°F with low humidity.
Turn regularly. Minimum 18 months; traditionally 36 months or more.

notes: AOP protected - made only in Central Switzerland
May be ancestor to Italian grana cheeses - traded over Alps for centuries
Extremely hard - eaten in thin shavings (Möckli), not grated
Lower moisture than any other Swiss cheese
The high cooking temperature creates dense, granular texture

recipes.title: Traditional Scamorza (Smoked Pear-Shaped Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Italian stretched-curd cheesemaking
recipes.description: A stretched-curd cheese from southern Italy, Scamorza is essentially mozzarella that's been hung to dry and develop flavor. The name means 'beheaded' referring to its pinched pear shape. Often smoked for additional flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C).
Add thermophilic culture, ripen 45-60 minutes.
Add rennet, stir gently, let set 30-40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Let curds rest under whey for 3-4 hours until pH reaches 5.2-5.3.
Test stretchability: small piece should stretch in hot water.
Cut acidified curd into strips.
Heat water to 170-175°F (77-80°C).
Stretch and knead curd until smooth and elastic.
Form into ball, then pinch and twist top to create pear shape with 'head.'
Tie string around neck for hanging.
Cool in cold salted water briefly.
Hang to dry for 24-48 hours.
For smoked scamorza: cold smoke for 2-4 hours with hardwood.
Continue aging hung in cool, ventilated space for 1-2 weeks.

notes: Fresh scamorza is white; smoked scamorza has golden-brown exterior
Texture is firmer and drier than mozzarella but still stretchy when heated
Excellent for grilling - holds shape while developing crispy exterior
Traditional in southern Italian cuisine, especially Molise and Campania
Can substitute for mozzarella when firmer texture desired

recipes.title: Traditional Selles-sur-Cher (French Ash-Rind Goat)
recipes.source_note: Named after the town of Selles-sur-Cher. The ash was originally used to protect the cheese from flies in farm cellars.
recipes.description: Small disc-shaped French goat cheese with a distinctive blue-gray ash rind, mild creamy interior, and delicate nutty flavor.

instructions.text: Warm goat milk to 68-72°F.
Add all cultures and stir gently.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 18-24 hours at room temperature until firm.
Ladle curds gently into flat disc molds (about 3.5 inches diameter, 1 inch deep).
Drain for 24-48 hours, flipping several times as curds compact.
Unmold and salt all surfaces lightly.
Let dry for several hours, then coat completely with ash.
Place in ripening area at 52-55°F, 85-90% humidity.
Turn every other day. Blue-gray mold grows through ash in 7-10 days.
Age for 2-3 weeks minimum until paste is creamy near rind.

notes: Traditional ash is from poplar wood, mixed with salt
The ash creates the distinctive blue-gray appearance as mold grows through it
Milder than many French goat cheeses - good introduction to chèvre
Best eaten young to medium aged - doesn't benefit from extended aging

recipes.title: Traditional Shanklish (Aged Levantine Herb Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Modernized from traditional Syrian/Lebanese methods, adapted for home cheesemaking
recipes.description: A remarkable aged cheese from Syria and Lebanon, shanklish begins as strained yogurt that's shaped into balls, dried, and aged with herbs and spices. The blue-gray mold that develops is prized, not feared. This ancient preservation technique creates an intensely flavored cheese.

instructions.text: Line a colander with several layers of cheesecloth. Pour yogurt into cloth and tie corners together.
Hang bundle over bowl and drain in refrigerator for 24-48 hours until very thick (labneh consistency).
Mix drained yogurt with salt. The texture should be like thick cream cheese.
Form mixture into balls about 1.5 inches in diameter. Place on a clean cloth-lined tray.
Air dry balls in a cool, dry place for 3-5 days, turning daily. They will form a dry skin.
For aged shanklish: Continue drying for 1-2 weeks. A blue-gray mold may develop - this is traditional and desirable.
Mix za'atar and Aleppo pepper. Roll dried cheese balls in the spice mixture to coat completely.
Store in a jar, covered with olive oil. Age at cool room temperature for 1-4 weeks for stronger flavor.
To serve, crumble or slice shanklish. Mix with diced tomatoes, onion, olive oil, and serve with flatbread.
Aged shanklish becomes pungent and crumbly, similar to blue cheese. It's an acquired taste prized by connoisseurs.

notes: The mold that develops is Penicillium, similar to blue cheese - it's safe and traditional
Fresh shanklish is mild; aged shanklish is very strong and pungent
Traditional in the Levant for using up excess yogurt
The spice coating helps control mold development and adds flavor
Can be made from goat or sheep milk yogurt for more authentic flavor

recipes.title: Traditional Shanklish (Syrian Aged Cheese Balls)
recipes.source_note: Ancient Levantine preservation method for cheese. The balls are rolled in zaatar and Aleppo pepper, creating a complex aged cheese.
recipes.description: Syrian and Lebanese aged cheese balls coated in thyme and red pepper, developing strong pungent flavors during fermentation.

instructions.text: Mix salt into thick labneh or strained yogurt.
Form into balls about 1.5 inches in diameter.
Place on a rack and let dry at room temperature for 3-5 days.
Turn balls daily. They will develop a dry crust and begin to ferment.
When balls are firm and slightly cracked on surface, mix zaatar and Aleppo pepper.
Roll each ball thoroughly in the spice mixture.
Place coated balls in a jar and cover completely with olive oil.
Age in a cool dark place for 2-4 weeks.
Cheese develops stronger, more pungent flavor with time.
Serve crumbled with olive oil, tomatoes, and flatbread.

notes: Shanklish is one of the oldest preserved cheese traditions in the Levant
The fermentation creates a strong blue cheese-like flavor
Traditional versions become quite pungent with extended aging
Can be stored in olive oil for many months

recipes.title: Traditional Sirene (Bulgarian White Brine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Bulgarian brine cheesemaking
recipes.description: Bulgaria's national cheese, Sirene has been made in the Balkans for thousands of years - possibly since Thracian times. This tangy, crumbly white cheese aged in brine is essential to Bulgarian cuisine and culture.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86-90°F (30-32°C).
Add mesophilic culture (or Bulgarian yogurt), ripen 45-60 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 45-60 minutes for soft curd.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes - relatively large.
Let curds rest under whey 15-20 minutes.
Gently stir and let curds settle again.
Drain curds and transfer to cloth-lined molds or colander.
Press lightly or let drain naturally for several hours.
Cut consolidated curd into blocks.
Prepare brine: dissolve 1 cup salt in 1 quart water (about 8-10% brine).
Submerge cheese blocks in brine.
Store at cool room temperature or refrigerate.
Ready in 30-60 days in brine. Keeps for months submerged.

recipes.temperature: 86-90°F (30-32°C) for make; store in brine at 40-50°F
notes: Similar to Greek feta but typically made from pure sheep's or cow's milk
Bulgarian yogurt cultures give characteristic tangy flavor
Essential in Shopska salad - the Bulgarian national dish
Sheep's milk version is richer; cow's milk is milder
Cheese preserved in brine keeps for many months

recipes.title: Traditional Spressa delle Giudicarie (Lean Ancient Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Italian low-fat cheesemaking
recipes.description: A unique 'poverty cheese' from the Giudicarie valleys of Trentino, made from skimmed milk after the cream was taken for butter. Despite humble origins, this medieval cheese developed complex flavors through long aging.

instructions.text: Let whole milk sit overnight so cream rises naturally.
Skim cream (save for butter), use remaining milk for cheese.
Heat skimmed milk to 93°F (34°C).
Add starter culture and ripen for 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, stir gently, let set for 30-40 minutes.
Cut curds into small 1/4-inch pieces.
Raise temperature slowly to 113°F (45°C) over 45 minutes.
Stir continuously as curds cook - this is crucial for texture.
Let curds settle, drain most whey.
Pack curds tightly into molds - no air pockets.
Press heavily: 40-50 lbs pressure for 24 hours, flipping several times.
Dry salt all surfaces generously.
Age at 50°F with 80% humidity for minimum 6 months.
Turn weekly, brush rind. Can age up to 24 months for intense flavor.

notes: Name means 'pressed' referring to heavy pressing technique
Low fat content requires longer aging for flavor development
DOP protected since 2003
Traditional wheels weigh 15-25 lbs and age up to 2 years
Has a distinctive 'squeaky' texture when young

recipes.title: Traditional Stilton (English King of Blues)
recipes.source_note: Named after the town of Stilton where it was sold, though never made there. PDO requires production in three specific counties.
recipes.description: English blue cheese with a crusty natural rind, creamy texture, and complex blue veining, considered England's finest blue.

instructions.text: Add cream to milk and heat to 86°F.
Add mesophilic culture and P. roqueforti. Ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 90 minutes until firm.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes.
Let curds settle, then ladle into cloth-lined mold without pressing.
Turn mold every 15 minutes for first 2 hours, then every hour for 24 hours.
Unmold and salt all surfaces daily for 5 days.
Smooth surface by hand-rubbing (or the sides with a knife).
Age at 55°F, 90% humidity.
Pierce with needles after 5-6 weeks to allow air for bluing.
Age 9-12 weeks total until blue veins develop throughout.

notes: Stilton is never pressed - the open texture is essential for bluing
PDO requires production only in Derbyshire, Leicestershire, or Nottinghamshire
The crusty brown rind develops naturally and is not washed
Traditionally served with port at Christmas

recipes.title: Traditional Stilton (English King of Cheeses)
recipes.source_note: Traditional English blue cheesemaking
recipes.description: England's most famous cheese, Stilton has been called the 'King of English Cheeses' since the 18th century. Made only in three counties, this rich, creamy blue develops its distinctive veins through careful aging.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C).
Add mesophilic culture and P. roqueforti. Ripen 60-90 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 90 minutes for very soft curd.
Cut curds into large cubes, let rest 15 minutes.
Ladle curds gently into draining trays - do not stir.
Let drain overnight, milling and turning the curd mass.
Mill curds by hand, salt thoroughly.
Pack loosely into tall cylindrical molds - no pressing.
Let drain 5-6 days, turning daily.
Smooth and seal surface by rubbing.
Age at 55°F with 90% humidity for 5-6 weeks.
Pierce with needles to encourage blue veining.
Continue aging 9-12 weeks total until proper blue development.

notes: PDO protected - can only be made in Derbyshire, Leicestershire, and Nottinghamshire
Never pressed - the open texture allows blue mold to develop
Traditional to pour port into the center (though purists debate this)
Should have creamy, golden paste with even blue-green veining
White Stilton (unblued) is also made and often flavored with fruit

recipes.title: Traditional Stinking Bishop (English Washed-Rind)
recipes.attribution: Gloucestershire, England / Modern Revival of Medieval
recipes.source_note: Revived by Charles Martell in 1972 based on medieval Cistercian recipes. Named after the Stinking Bishop pear used to wash the rind.
recipes.description: Pungent English washed-rind cheese made from Gloucester cattle milk and washed with perry, with a soft creamy interior.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F.
Add mesophilic culture and B. linens. Stir gently and ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 1 hour.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes.
Stir gently for 30 minutes at 86°F.
Ladle curds into round mold. Press lightly for 4 hours, flipping twice.
Salt all surfaces and let dry at room temperature for 1-2 days.
Move to cave at 55°F, 95% humidity.
Wash rind with perry every 2-3 days.
Continue washing for 6-8 weeks until rind is orange-pink and pungent.
Interior should be soft and bulging when ripe.

notes: The perry (pear cider) wash creates the distinctive aroma
Named after the Stinking Bishop pear variety, not an ecclesiastic
Featured in Wallace & Gromit's 'The Curse of the Were-Rabbit'
One of England's most pungent cheeses

recipes.title: Traditional Stracchino (Italian 'Tired Cow' Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Name comes from 'stracca' (tired) - made from milk of cows tired from their descent from alpine pastures.
recipes.description: Italian soft, spreadable cheese with a mild, milky flavor and creamy, slightly runny texture when ripe.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F.
Add mesophilic culture and ripen 30 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then small amount of diluted rennet.
Let set for 45-60 minutes until soft curd forms.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes.
Let rest 10 minutes, then gently ladle into flat rectangular molds.
Let drain at room temperature for 24 hours, turning several times.
Salt surfaces.
Age at 50-55°F, 90% humidity for 1-3 weeks.
Cheese becomes softer and more spreadable as it ages.

notes: Made from milk of cows fatigued from alpine descent (transhumance)
Tired cows produce richer milk with higher fat content
Related to Gorgonzola and Taleggio
Best eaten young when still fresh and mild

recipes.title: Traditional Sulguni (Georgian Stretched Cheese)
recipes.source_note: From the Samegrelo region of Georgia, where cheesemaking traditions date back thousands of years. Related to Italian pasta filata.
recipes.description: Georgian brine-soaked stretched cheese with a layered structure and mild salty flavor, often smoked or filled with other cheeses.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add culture and let ripen 30 minutes.
Add rennet and let set for 45 minutes.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes.
Drain whey and let curds acidify at room temperature for 6-12 hours.
Test curd by stretching a piece in hot water - when it stretches smoothly, it's ready.
Heat water to 170-180°F. Cut curd into strips.
Submerge strips in hot water and stretch, folding repeatedly.
Form into round flat discs about 1 inch thick.
Place in cold water briefly to set shape.
Make brine and soak cheese for 12-24 hours.
Store in brine. Optionally smoke for smoked sulguni.

notes: Sulguni is essential for Georgian khachapuri bread
The layered stretched structure is visible when sliced
Can be filled with fresh curd cheese (gadazelili sulguni)
Smoked sulguni is popular throughout the Caucasus

recipes.title: Traditional Sulguni (Georgian Stretched Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Georgian pasta filata cheesemaking
recipes.description: Georgia's most famous cheese, Sulguni is a stretched-curd cheese from the Samegrelo region. Similar to mozzarella but traditionally stored in brine, it can be fresh, smoked, or braided. Essential to Georgian cuisine.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 95°F (35°C).
Add starter or kefir, ripen 30 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 30-40 minutes.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch pieces.
Let curds acidify under whey for 3-5 hours until pH 5.2-5.3.
Test: small piece should stretch in hot water.
Heat water to 170-175°F (77-80°C).
Cut curd into strips, submerge in hot water.
Knead and stretch until smooth and elastic.
Form into flat disc shape (traditional) or braid.
Cool in cold water, then transfer to brine.
Store in brine refrigerated. Can be smoked for extra flavor.

notes: PGI protected from Georgia's Samegrelo region
Can be fresh, brined, smoked, or braided
Smoked Sulguni has distinctive golden-brown surface
Essential for khachapuri (Georgian cheese bread)
Stretchy texture but firmer than Italian mozzarella

recipes.title: Traditional Taleggio (Italian Cave-Aged Washed-Rind)
recipes.source_note: Named after the Val Taleggio valley where it originated. Aged in caves for the cool humid conditions.
recipes.description: Italian washed-rind cheese with a pungent orange rind, soft creamy interior, and tangy fruity flavor.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F.
Add mesophilic culture and B. linens. Ripen 45 minutes.
Add calcium chloride if needed, then diluted rennet.
Let set for 1 hour.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes.
Stir very gently for 10 minutes at 90°F.
Ladle curds into square molds (8x8 inches).
Turn frequently for 24 hours, letting drain naturally.
Salt and dry for 2 days.
Age at 50-55°F, 95% humidity.
Wash with brine every 2-3 days.
Age 5-7 weeks until rind is orange and paste is soft.

notes: Traditionally aged in the caves of Val Taleggio
The square shape with distinctive 'T' stamp identifies authentic Taleggio
Pungent aroma belies a mild, fruity taste
DOP protected since 1988

recipes.title: Traditional Teleme (California Portuguese Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional California artisan cheesemaking
recipes.description: Brought to California by Portuguese immigrants, Teleme is a creamy, tangy cheese that softens dramatically as it ages. Made in the San Joaquin Valley since the early 1900s, it's California's hidden gem.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F (32°C).
Add extra mesophilic culture for tangier cheese. Ripen 45-60 minutes.
Add diluted rennet (use less than usual for softer curd).
Let set 45-60 minutes until soft curd forms.
Cut curds into large 1-inch cubes - handle gently.
Let curds rest 15 minutes, then stir very gently.
Drain whey and ladle curds into molds without pressing.
Let drain naturally 24 hours, flipping several times.
Salt surfaces lightly.
Dust with rice flour (traditional) to prevent sticking.
Age at 50°F with high humidity for 2-8 weeks.
Cheese becomes increasingly soft and tangy with age.

notes: Rice flour coating is traditional California twist
Named for Romanian 'telemea' brought by Portuguese via Brazil
Should become quite soft and spreadable when well-aged
Franklin Peluso family made it famous in Los Banos, CA
Tangy, lactic flavor intensifies with age

recipes.title: Traditional Telemea (Romanian Fresh Brine Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Romanian brine cheesemaking
recipes.description: Romania's beloved white brine cheese, Telemea has been made by shepherds in the Carpathian Mountains for centuries. Softer and creamier than Bulgarian sirene, it's essential to Romanian cuisine and pastoral culture.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (30°C).
Add mesophilic culture, ripen 30-45 minutes.
Add diluted rennet, let set 45-60 minutes for soft curd.
Cut curds into large 2-inch cubes.
Let curds rest undisturbed 15-20 minutes.
Very gently ladle curds into cloth-lined mold.
Let drain naturally - no pressing - for 8-12 hours.
Turn mold several times during draining.
Unmold and cut into blocks.
Prepare lighter brine: about 6-8% salt solution.
Submerge cheese blocks in brine.
Ready in 14-30 days. Keep refrigerated in brine.

recipes.temperature: 86°F (30°C) for make; store in brine at 35-45°F
notes: Softer and creamier than Greek feta or Bulgarian sirene
PDO Telemea de Ibăneşti made only in Mureş County
Sheep's milk version from Carpathian pastures is most prized
Essential in Romanian mămăligă (polenta) dishes
Traditional preservation method for mountain shepherds

recipes.title: Traditional Tilsit (German Baltic Cheese)
recipes.source_note: Traditional German/Swiss cheesemaking
